S065.name: Obsessions
S065.description: Recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as intrusive and unwanted, and attempts to ignore or suppress them.

subtypes.Contamination Obsessions: Recurrent and intrusive worries about contamination, germs, or dirt.
subtypes.Pathological Doubt: Pathological doubt regarding safety or mistakes, such as whether doors are locked or gas valves are closed.
subtypes.Symmetry and Exactness Obsessions: A strong urge that items must be lined up exactly or be symmetrical.
subtypes.Forbidden or Taboo Thoughts: Intrusive thoughts involving aggressive (harming others), sexual, or religious content that are prohibited.
subtypes.Somatic Obsessions: Persistent and specific fear that one might have a serious disease.

S066.name: Compulsions
S066.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to an obsession or to prevent anxiety/distress; clearly excessive or not realistically connected.

subtypes.Cleaning or Washing Compulsions: Repetitive acts to remove contamination, such as hand washing, showering, or excessive cleaning.
subtypes.Checking Compulsions: Repeatedly checking items like door locks, gas stoves, or switches to prevent danger.
subtypes.Ordering and Arranging Compulsions: Organizing objects in a specific order or at a precise angle to reduce anxiety.
subtypes.Mental Acts: Mental rituals performed internally, such as praying, counting, or repeating specific words silently.
subtypes.Repeating Rituals: Repeating specific actions (e.g., standing up, passing through a door) a set number of times.

symptom.disease_info: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder is defined by intrusive, unwanted obsessions and/or repetitive compulsions performed to reduce distress or prevent feared outcomes, with the pattern becoming time-consuming or functionally impairing. It often has a gradual course that may worsen under stress, and it is distinguished from ordinary perfectionism or worry by the ego-dystonic quality of the thoughts and the excessive, ritualized responses.

patient.stressor: Hector lost a close friend from his salsa and tech-meetup circle unexpectedly, and the death unsettled the dependable structure he had built around work, community events, and late-night social rituals. In the period that followed, intrusive thoughts about preventable harm and personal responsibility became increasingly difficult for him to set aside, and he responded with repeated reviews, checks, and mental rituals that spread from his private life into his management of cybersecurity and infrastructure projects. The pattern escalated until he was staying at the office long after others left, missing basketball and dance commitments, and jeopardizing a major cloud migration because he could not stop re-verifying decisions. After a serious deadline failure and visible deterioration in his functioning, his company’s occupational health program helped arrange urgent psychiatric care.

S065.name: Obsessions
S065.description: Recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as intrusive and unwanted, and attempts to ignore or suppress them.
S065.manifestation: What brings me in is that I keep getting these thoughts that if I miss one setting, one access rule, one warning sign, someone could get hurt or lose everything, and even though part of me knows it’s irrational, it hits me like I’m personally responsible and I can’t just move on.

S066.name: Compulsions
S066.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to an obsession or to prevent anxiety/distress; clearly excessive or not realistically connected.
S066.manifestation: I’ll reread deployment plans, audit logs, door locks, and even old messages over and over, sometimes counting through steps in my head until they feel 'safe,' and I’ve stayed at the office for hours after everyone leaves because stopping before it feels complete makes me panic.

add_requirements.functional_impairment: I missed a major cloud migration deadline because I couldn’t finish signing off on decisions, and my team has started working around me instead of relying on me. I’ve also stopped showing up for basketball and salsa nights, so I’m losing the routines and people that used to keep me grounded.
